title: Merge Sorted Array
statement_short: Given two integer arrays sorted in non-decreasing order, merge the second array into the first array as a single sorted array in-place. The first array has additional empty space at the end to accommodate all elements.
hint: Small n and m do not restrict time complexity, but in-place merging requires O(1) extra space.
why_not: Right: Two Pointers iterating backward from the ends of both arrays merge elements in-place in O(m+n) time. Not Sorting: Concatenating and sorting takes O((m+n) log(m+n)) time. Not Heap / Priority Queue: Inserting all elements into a min-heap takes O((m+n) log(m+n)) time and extra space. Not HashMap / Hash Set: Hash tables do not preserve order and incur unnecessary space overhead.

title: Remove Element
statement_short: Given an integer array and a target value, remove all occurrences of that target value in-place. Return the number of elements remaining after placing valid elements in the front of the array.
constraints: 0 <= nums.length <= 50, 0 <= nums[i] <= 50, 0 <= val <= 100
hint: Small array size places no time restriction, but elements must be overwritten in-place with O(1) space.
why_not: Right: Two Pointers (read and write indices) overwrite target values in a single O(n) pass in-place. Not Sliding Window: The task requires modifying array elements across the entire array, not identifying an optimal continuous window. Not HashMap / Hash Set: Using a hash set requires O(n) auxiliary space, violating the in-place constraint. Not Stack: Pushing valid elements to a stack consumes O(n) extra memory.

title: Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array
statement_short: Given an integer array sorted in non-decreasing order, remove duplicates in-place so that each unique element appears only once while keeping their relative order. Return the count of unique elements.
hint: Input length up to 3 * 10^4 requires an O(n) time solution, while sorted order enables linear in-place tracking.
why_not: Right: Two Pointers exploit sorted order to overwrite adjacent duplicates in-place in O(n) time. Not HashMap / Hash Set: A hash set identifies unique items but uses unnecessary O(n) space. Not Binary Search: Binary search locates values in logarithmic time but cannot perform in-place array compaction. Not Monotonic Stack: Stack tracking is unnecessary because the input array is already sorted.

title: Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array II
statement_short: Given a sorted integer array, remove excess duplicates in-place such that each unique element appears at most twice while preserving relative order. Return the updated array length.
hint: Input size up to 3 * 10^4 requires O(n) time, and pre-sorted order permits fixed-offset duplicate checks.
why_not: Right: Two Pointers compare the reader element against writer-2 to allow at most two copies in-place in O(n) time. Not 1D DP: Dynamic programming transitions are unnecessary for simple conditional array overwrite. Not Sliding Window: The problem asks for modifying sequence elements, not finding a max/min subsegment window. Not HashMap / Hash Set: Tracking element frequencies in a hash map uses O(n) auxiliary space.

title: Majority Element
statement_short: Given an array of size n, find the element that appears more than floor(n / 2) times. You may assume that the majority element always exists in the input array.
hint: Input size up to 5 * 10^4 requires O(n) time, and the guaranteed majority property enables O(1) space element cancellation.
why_not: Right: Boyer-Moore Voting pairs majority and minority items to cancel non-majority elements in O(n) time and O(1) space. Not Sorting: Sorting puts the majority element at index n/2 but costs O(n log n) time. Not HashMap / Hash Set: Frequency counting takes O(n) time but requires O(n) extra space. Not Bit Manipulation: Bitwise counting takes O(32n) time, which is slower than linear voting.

title: Rotate Array
statement_short: Given an integer array nums, rotate the array to the right by k steps, where k is non-negative. Perform the rotation in-place with O(1) extra space.
hint: n up to 10^5 dictates an O(n) time algorithm, and in-place requirements favor index swapping via array reversals.
keywords: rotate the array to the right
why_not: Right: Two Pointers reverses the whole array and then reverses two sub-parts using double-pointer swaps in O(n) time and O(1) space. Not 1D DP: Subproblem state caching is unnecessary for cyclic index permutations. Not HashMap / Hash Set: Mapping original indices to new locations uses O(n) extra memory. Not Sorting: Sorting alters element value ordering rather than performing cyclic shift placement.

title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock
statement_short: Given an array of stock prices where prices[i] is the price on the i-th day, find the maximum profit from buying on one day and selling on a future day. Return 0 if no profit can be achieved.
constraints: 1 <= prices.length <= 10^5, 0 <= prices[i] <= 10^4
hint: Array size up to 10^5 requires an O(n) time solution by maintaining the lowest price seen so far in a single pass.
keywords: buying on one day and selling on a future day
why_not: Right: Greedy tracks the minimum buying price seen so far and updates maximum profit at each day in O(n) time and O(1) space. Not 2D DP: Maintaining a full state matrix is redundant for a single buy-sell transaction. Not Two Pointers: Scanning inward from both ends misses peak profit points occurring within inner subsegments. Not Monotonic Stack: Maintaining a monotonic price stack consumes unnecessary O(n) extra space.

title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock II
statement_short: Given an integer array prices, find the maximum total profit achieved by completing as many stock transactions as you like. You may only hold at most one share of the stock at any time.
constraints: 1 <= prices.length <= 3 \* 10^4, 0 <= prices[i] <= 10^4
hint: Limit of 3 \* 10^4 demands an O(n) single pass, accumulating positive price differences between consecutive days.
keywords: as many stock transactions as you like
why_not: Right: Greedy sums every positive daily price increase (prices[i] - prices[i-1]) to capture all profitable upward slopes in O(n) time. Not Backtracking: Exploring all transaction decision combinations results in O(2^n) exponential time. Not Intervals: Merging transaction intervals adds unnecessary complexity when daily differences suffice. Not Binary Search: Price values are not sorted, so binary search cannot determine transaction points.

title: Jump Game
statement_short: Given an integer array nums where each element represents your maximum jump length from that position, determine if you can reach the last index starting from index 0.
constraints: 1 <= nums.length <= 10^4, 0 <= nums[i] <= 10^5
hint: Array length up to 10^4 requires an O(n) solution by continually expanding the furthest reachable index.
why_not: Right: Greedy maintains the maximum reachable index while scanning left-to-right in O(n) time and O(1) space. Not Graph BFS: Level-by-level queue traversal visits reachable nodes but uses O(n) auxiliary memory. Not Backtracking: Trying every jump branch recursively causes TLE with O(2^n) exponential complexity. Not 2D DP: A two-dimensional state space is unnecessary for tracking a single reachability boundary.

title: Jump Game II
statement_short: Given a 0-indexed array of non-negative integers nums where nums[i] represents your max jump length at index i, return the minimum number of jumps required to reach the last index.
constraints: 1 <= nums.length <= 10^4, 0 <= nums[i] <= 1000, answer is guaranteed
hint: Input size up to 10^4 requires O(n) time, reachable by updating jump range boundaries greedily.
keywords: max jump length at index i
why_not: Right: Greedy tracks current jump range end and furthest reachable index to increment jump count in O(n) time and O(1) space. Not 1D DP: DP computing min jumps to each index takes O(n^2) time in the worst case. Not Graph DFS: DFS explores all paths to the end, resulting in exponential search overhead. Not Binary Search: Jump boundaries are non-monotonic, so binary search cannot find min jumps directly.

title: H-Index
statement_short: Given an array of citations for a researcher's papers, compute the researcher's h-index. The h-index is the maximum value h such that the researcher has published at least h papers that have each been cited at least h times.
constraints: 1 <= citations.length <= 5000, 0 <= citations[i] <= 1000
hint: Array length up to 5000 allows O(n log n) sorting or O(n) bucket counting to locate the citation threshold.
why_not: Right: Sorting citations in descending order allows finding the largest index i where citations[i] >= i + 1 in O(n log n) time. Not Binary Search on Answer: Binary search on h from 0 to n works in O(n log n) time but is more complex than sorting directly. Not HashMap / Hash Set: Using a bucket array works in O(n) space, but general hash maps add unneeded hashing overhead. Not Heap / Priority Queue: Maintaining a min-heap of size h takes O(n log h) time and O(n) auxiliary space.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(1) space

title: Insert Delete GetRandom O(1)
statement_short: Design a data structure that supports inserting a value, removing a value, and obtaining a random element, all in average O(1) time. Each element must have an equal probability of being returned by the random operation.
constraints: -2^31 <= val <= 2^31 - 1, at most 2 \* 10^5 calls will be made to insert, remove, and getRandom
hint: The O(1) average time requirement for search combined with uniform random selection mandates combining a hash map with a dynamic array.
why_not: Right: HashMap / Hash Set maps values to array indices, enabling O(1) deletion via swap-with-last element and O(1) random array access. Not Heap / Priority Queue: Deleting an arbitrary value or getting a random element from a heap takes O(n) time. Not Binary Search: Binary search requires a sorted structure, making O(1) arbitrary insertion and random sampling impossible. Not Two Pointers: Two pointers require linear scanning for value lookups and deletions.

title: Product of Array Except Self
statement_short: Given an integer array nums, return an array answer such that answer[i] is equal to the product of all the elements of nums except nums[i]. You must write an algorithm that runs in O(n) time without using the division operation.
constraints: 2 <= nums.length <= 10^5, -30 <= nums[i] <= 30, product of any prefix or suffix is guaranteed to fit in 32-bit integer
hint: Array size up to 10^5 demands O(n) time, while the division ban requires accumulating prefix and suffix products.
why_not: Right: Prefix Sum (extended to prefix and suffix products) combines left-accumulated and right-accumulated products in O(n) time and O(1) extra space. Not Two Pointers: Two pointers cannot compute products for every position except the current index in O(n) total operations. Not Sliding Window: The product excludes a single element rather than calculating range aggregates over contiguous subsegments. Not Monotonic Stack: Maintaining monotonic order does not aid in multiplying all non-current elements.

title: Gas Station
statement_short: There are n gas stations along a circular route, where the gas at the i-th station is gas[i] and the cost to travel to the next station is cost[i]. Return the starting gas station's index if you can travel around the circuit once in the clockwise direction, otherwise return -1.
constraints: n == gas.length == cost.length, 1 <= n <= 10^5, 0 <= gas[i], cost[i] <= 10^4
hint: n up to 10^5 dictates an O(n) single pass, resetting the starting station whenever cumulative tank balance drops below zero.
why_not: Right: Greedy checks if total gas >= total cost and advances the candidate start index past any station where running gas balance turns negative in O(n) time. Not Graph BFS: Simulating full circular traversals from every node takes O(n^2) time. Not Sliding Window: The circular traversal length is fixed to n rather than finding a variable subsegment. Not 2D DP: Multi-dimensional state tracking is unnecessary for cumulative net balance evaluation.

title: Candy
statement_short: There are n children standing in a line, each with a rating value given in an integer array ratings. Each child must receive at least one candy, and children with a higher rating than their neighbors must get more candies than their neighbors. Return the minimum total candies required.
constraints: n == ratings.length, 1 <= n <= 2 \* 10^4, 0 <= ratings[i] <= 2 \* 10^4
hint: n up to 2 \* 10^4 requires O(n) time, achievable via left-to-right and right-to-left greedy distribution passes.
why_not: Right: Greedy satisfies neighbor rating constraints by making a left-to-right pass followed by a right-to-left pass in O(n) time and O(n) space. Not 1D DP: Dynamic programming subproblem state transitions collapse into localized neighbor comparison passes. Not Heap / Priority Queue: Processing children in increasing order of ratings takes O(n log n) time and extra space. Not Monotonic Stack: Monotonic stack tracking is unnecessary since neighbor constraints depend strictly on immediate adjacent values.

title: Trapping Rain Water
statement_short: Given n non-negative integers representing an elevation map where the width of each bar is 1, compute how much water it can trap after raining.
constraints: n == height.length, 1 <= n <= 2 \* 10^4, 0 <= height[i] <= 10^5
hint: n up to 2 \* 10^4 requires O(n) time, which two pointers achieve by tracking max left and right boundaries inward in O(1) space.
keywords: how much water it can trap
why_not: Right: Two Pointers inward scan calculates trapped water based on min(left_max, right_max) in O(n) time and O(1) space. Not Monotonic Stack: Monotonic stack also solves this in O(n) time by bounded horizontal layers, but uses O(n) auxiliary space. Not Sliding Window: The trapped water depends on global maximum boundaries rather than a fixed sliding window size. Not Binary Search on Answer: The total water volume cannot be verified easily using binary search on a target result.

title: Roman to Integer
statement_short: Given a Roman numeral string s, convert it to an integer. Roman numerals are represented by seven different symbols, where subtractive combinations occur when a smaller value precedes a larger value.
constraints: 1 <= s.length <= 15, s contains only characters ('I', 'V', 'X', 'L', 'C', 'D', 'M'), s is a valid roman numeral in range [1, 3999]
hint: Extremely small string length (s.length <= 15) allows a single-pass character map lookup with conditional subtraction.
keywords: smaller value precedes a larger value
why_not: Right: Math / Geometry applies numeral symbol values and subtractive rules (subtracting when current symbol < next symbol) in O(n) time. Not HashMap / Hash Set: Using a hash table maps symbols to values, but the core logic is linear arithmetic symbol parsing. Not Stack: Pushing symbols to a stack handles nesting, but simple left-to-right symbol value comparisons require no stack frame. Not Backtracking: Roman numerals follow deterministic grammar rules, requiring no recursive branch search.

title: Integer to Roman
statement_short: Given an integer num, convert it to a Roman numeral string. Symbol values are processed from largest to smallest, using subtractive form rules for values starting with 4 or 9.
hint: Small bounded input range (num <= 3999) allows greedy subtraction using a pre-defined array of value-symbol pairs.
keywords: convert it to a Roman numeral string
why_not: Right: Greedy repeatedly subtracts the largest matching Roman numeral value from num to construct the result string in O(1) time. Not Math / Geometry: Pure digit extraction works, but greedy matching against symbol tables is far cleaner. Not 1D DP: Storing state transitions is unnecessary because the greedy choice is always globally optimal. Not Trie: Prefix trees store string dictionaries, which do not apply to integer conversion.

title: Length of Last Word
statement_short: Given a string s consisting of words and spaces, return the length of the last word in s. A word is a maximal substring consisting of non-space characters only.
constraints: 1 <= s.length <= 10^4, s consists of English letters and spaces ' ', s contains at least one word
hint: String length up to 10^4 allows an O(n) reverse scan, skipping trailing spaces then counting word characters.
why_not: Right: Two Pointers (or reverse linear scan) skips trailing space characters and counts consecutive letter characters in O(n) time and O(1) space. Not Sliding Window: Finding the last word requires scanning backward from the end rather than managing a forward sliding subsegment. Not Stack: Pushing characters or words onto a stack uses O(n) extra memory needlessly. Not HashMap / Hash Set: Word lookup tables are irrelevant for a simple string index traversal.

title: Longest Common Prefix
statement_short: Given an array of strings, write a function to find the longest common prefix string amongst an array of strings. Return an empty string if there is no common prefix.
constraints: 1 <= strs.length <= 200, 0 <= strs[i].length <= 200, strs[i] consists of only lowercase English letters
hint: Small array and string lengths (length <= 200) allow O(S) horizontal or vertical character comparison.
keywords: empty string if there is no common prefix
why_not: Right: Two Pointers (vertical/horizontal character scanning) compares characters at index i across strings in O(S) time and O(1) space. Not Trie: Building a prefix tree also finds the longest common prefix in O(S) time, but uses extra O(S) space. Not Binary Search: Binary search on prefix length takes O(S log m) time, which is slower than linear scanning. Not HashMap / Hash Set: Hash tables do not optimize character-by-character prefix matching.

title: Reverse Words in a String
statement_short: Given an input string s containing words separated by spaces, reverse the order of the words. Return a string of the words joined by a single space with no leading or trailing spaces.
constraints: 1 <= s.length <= 10^4, s contains English letters, digits, and spaces ' ', at least one word
hint: String length up to 10^4 requires an O(n) algorithm, achievable in-place using two-pointer segment reversals.
keywords: reverse the order of the words
why_not: Right: Two Pointers reverses the whole character sequence and then reverses each individual word in-place in O(n) time and O(1) extra space. Not Stack: Pushing words onto a stack reverses word order but consumes O(n) auxiliary memory. Not Sliding Window: The task modifies word sequence order rather than maintaining a continuous subsegment. Not HashMap / Hash Set: Hash tables do not assist with word position swaps or string reversal.

title: Zigzag Conversion
statement_short: Given a string s and a number of rows, write s in a zigzag pattern across the rows and read line by line. Return the concatenated string formed by reading the rows top to bottom.
constraints: 1 <= s.length <= 1000, 1 <= numRows <= 1000, s consists of English letters, commas, and periods
hint: Small string length (<= 1000) permits row-by-row character placement or direct arithmetic index mapping.
keywords: reading the rows top to bottom
why_not: Right: Math / Geometry calculates row character indices directly using cycle length formula 2\*(numRows-1) in O(n) time. Not 2D DP: Grid dynamic programming is over-engineering for deterministic index arithmetic. Not Two Pointers: Scanning from both string ends does not determine row-by-row character ordering. Not Stack: LIFO processing does not preserve the top-to-bottom row sequence.

title: Find the Index of the First Occurrence in a String
statement_short: Given two strings needle and haystack, return the index of the first occurrence of needle in haystack. Return -1 if needle is not part of haystack.
constraints: 1 <= haystack.length, needle.length <= 10^4, haystack and needle consist of lowercase English letters
hint: String lengths up to 10^4 permit O(n+m) linear search using matching pointers.
keywords: needle is not part of haystack
why_not: Right: Two Pointers (or Knuth-Morris-Pratt pattern matching) finds the target occurrence in O(n+m) time and O(1) space. Not Sliding Window: Sliding a fixed window takes O(n\*m) worst-case time without mismatch shift optimization. Not Binary Search: String characters are unsorted, preventing binary search comparisons. Not Trie: Building a prefix tree uses O(m) extra memory for a single target string.

title: Text Justification
statement_short: Given an array of words and a maximum line width, format the text such that each line has exactly maxWidth characters and is fully justified. Distribute extra spaces as evenly as possible between words, placing remaining spaces on the left.
constraints: 1 <= words.length <= 300, 1 <= words[i].length <= 20, 1 <= maxWidth <= 100
hint: Small word count (<= 300) allows line-by-line greedy word packing and explicit space distribution.
keywords: extra spaces as evenly as possible
why_not: Right: Greedy packs maximum possible words onto each line before formatting spaces in O(n) total time. Not 1D DP: Dynamic programming optimizes line breaks under quadratic penalty functions, but problem rules specify greedy line filling. Not Two Pointers: Scanning word indices alone does not implement space padding logic. Not Backtracking: Line construction follows explicit greedy formatting rules, requiring no recursive path search.

title: Valid Palindrome
statement_short: Given a string s, determine if it is a palindrome after converting all uppercase letters into lowercase letters and removing all non-alphanumeric characters. Read forwards and backwards identically.
constraints: 1 <= s.length <= 2 \* 10^5, s consists only of printable ASCII characters
hint: String length up to 2 \* 10^5 mandates an O(n) time solution, achieved by inward scanning pointers.
why_not: Right: Two Pointers compare valid alphanumeric characters inward from opposite string ends in O(n) time and O(1) space. Not Stack: Pushing valid characters onto a stack reverses the string but uses O(n) extra space. Not Sliding Window: Palindrome checking evaluates boundary characters moving inward rather than maintaining a fixed subsegment. Not HashMap / Hash Set: Character frequency tables verify anagrams, not palindrome character ordering.

title: Is Subsequence
statement_short: Given two strings s and t, return true if s is a subsequence of t, or false otherwise. A subsequence is formed by deleting some characters without disturbing the relative positions of the remaining characters.
constraints: 0 <= s.length <= 100, 0 <= t.length <= 10^4, s and t consist of lowercase English letters
hint: Target length t up to 10^4 requires an O(|t|) single pass using two pointer matching.
why_not: Right: Two Pointers advance along t while matching target characters from s in O(|t|) time and O(1) space. Not 1D DP: Dynamic programming checks longest common subsequence in O(|s|\*|t|) time, which is slower than linear matching. Not Binary Search: Binary search on character index lists optimizes multi-query s searches, but two pointers is optimal for single checks. Not HashMap / Hash Set: Hash tables track character frequencies but lose relative character ordering.

title: Two Sum II - Input Array Is Sorted
statement_short: Given a 1-indexed array of integers numbers that is already sorted in non-decreasing order, find two numbers that add up to a specific target number. Return their indices using 1-based indexing.
constraints: 2 <= numbers.length <= 3 \* 10^4, -1000 <= numbers[i] <= 1000, numbers is sorted in non-decreasing order, exactly one solution
hint: Sorted input with n up to 3 \* 10^4 mandates an O(n) solution using opposite-end pointers with O(1) space.
why_not: Right: Two Pointers shrink inward from opposite ends based on sum comparison in O(n) time and O(1) space. Not HashMap / Hash Set: Storing values in a hash map solves Two Sum in O(n) time but consumes unnecessary O(n) auxiliary space. Not Binary Search: Binary searching the complement for each element takes O(n log n) time, which is slower than two pointers. Not Prefix Sum: Prefix sums calculate cumulative range totals, not target pair sums.

title: Container With Most Water
statement_short: Given an integer array height of length n, find two lines that together with the x-axis form a container such that the container contains the most water. Return the maximum volume of water stored.
constraints: n == height.length, 2 <= n <= 10^5, 0 <= height[i] <= 10^4
hint: n up to 10^5 demands an O(n) single pass, shrinking the pointer at the shorter boundary greedily.
why_not: Right: Two Pointers start at outer boundaries and move the shorter height inward, evaluating max area in O(n) time and O(1) space. Not Monotonic Stack: Monotonic stack tracks trapped water between bars (LC 42), not maximum container area between two arbitrary lines. Not Sliding Window: The container width shrinks from full width inward rather than sliding a fixed/growing contiguous subsegment. Not Greedy: Pure greedy choice without boundary movement logic fails to explore all candidate area bottlenecks.

title: 3Sum
statement_short: Given an integer array nums, return all unique triplets [nums[i], nums[j], nums[k]] such that i != j, i != k, and j != k, and their sum equals zero.
constraints: 3 <= nums.length <= 3000, -10^5 <= nums[i] <= 10^5
hint: Array length up to 3000 permits an O(n^2) algorithm by sorting and fixing one number then using two pointers.
why_not: Right: Sorting and applying Two Pointers for each fixed element finds unique triplets in O(n^2) time and O(1) extra space. Not HashMap / Hash Set: Using nested loops with a hash set takes O(n^2) time but uses O(n) space and requires complex duplicate triplet filtering. Not Backtracking: Exploring combinations recursively leads to TLE with O(2^n) time complexity. Not Binary Search: Binary search for the third element takes O(n^2 log n) time, which is slower than two pointers.

title: Minimum Size Subarray Sum
statement_short: Given an array of positive integers nums and a positive integer target, return the minimal length of a contiguous subarray whose sum is greater than or equal to target. If there is no such subarray, return 0.
constraints: 1 <= target <= 10^9, 1 <= nums.length <= 10^5, 1 <= nums[i] <= 10^5
hint: Array length up to 10^5 and positive numbers permit an O(n) variable-size sliding window.
keywords: minimal length of a contiguous subarray
greater than or equal to target
why_not: Right: Sliding Window expands right pointer to reach sum >= target and contracts left pointer to minimize window size in O(n) time. Not Prefix Sum: Prefix sums combined with binary search solve this in O(n log n) time, which is slower than sliding window. Not Binary Search on Answer: Binary searching window length takes O(n log n) time, which is less optimal than linear sliding window. Not Two Pointers: Scanning fixed ends doesn't handle contiguous subarray window expansion for positive arrays as naturally.

title: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
statement_short: Given a string s, find the length of the longest substring without repeating characters.
constraints: 0 <= s.length <= 5 \* 10^4, s consists of English letters, digits, symbols and spaces
hint: String length up to 5 \* 10^4 demands an O(n) time solution using a variable sliding window.
why_not: Right: Sliding Window maintains a range of distinct characters using a set/map, expanding right and shrinking left on duplicates in O(n) time. Not HashMap / Hash Set: Using a hash set alone without a sliding window frame requires checking all O(n^2) substrings. Not Two Pointers: Scanning fixed ends inward cannot track variable non-repeating subsegments. Not 1D DP: Dynamic programming requires O(n) space and extra state transitions compared to direct sliding window pointers.

title: Substring with Concatenation of All Words
statement_short: Given a string s and an array of strings words of equal length, find all starting indices of substrings in s that are a concatenation of each word in words exactly once.
constraints: 1 <= s.length <= 10^4, 1 <= words.length <= 5000, 1 <= words[i].length <= 30
hint: Fixed word length allows running k sliding windows of step size k to check word frequency matches.
why_not: Right: Sliding Window over word-length steps tracks word frequency matches in O(n \* k) time using a frequency map. Not HashMap / Hash Set: Checking every substring independently with hash maps takes O(n \* m \* k) time without sliding window reuse. complexity: O(n \* k) time, O(m \* k) space

title: Minimum Window Substring
statement_short: Given two strings s and t, return the minimum window substring of s such that every character in t (including duplicates) is included in the window. Return an empty string if no such window exists.
constraints: 1 <= s.length, t.length <= 10^5, s and t consist of uppercase and lowercase English letters
hint: Lengths up to 10^5 mandate an O(n) sliding window that expands right to satisfy frequency and contracts left to minimize length.

Not Monotonic Stack: Monotonic order tracking does not handle multi-character frequency matching.

title: Valid Sudoku
statement_short: Determine if a 9x9 Sudoku board is valid. Only the filled cells must be validated according to the rules: each row, column, and 3x3 sub-box must contain digits 1-9 without repetition.
constraints: board.length == 9, board[i].length == 9, board[i][j] is a digit '1'-'9' or '.'
hint: Fixed 9x9 board size implies constant time verification using hash sets for rows, columns, and sub-boxes.

title: Spiral Matrix
statement_short: Given an m x n matrix, return all elements of the matrix in spiral order.
constraints: m == matrix.length, n == matrix[i].length, 1 <= m, n <= 10, -100 <= matrix[i][j] <= 100
hint: Small matrix size (<= 10x10) allows simulating spiral traversal by shrinking four boundary pointers.
why_not: Right: Two Pointers (four boundary pointers: top, bottom, left, right) shrink inward to traverse all matrix elements in O(m \* n) time and O(1) extra space. title: Rotate Image
statement_short: Given an n x n 2D matrix representing an image, rotate the image by 90 degrees clockwise in-place.
constraints: n == matrix.length == matrix[i].length, 1 <= n <= 20, -1000 <= matrix[i][j] <= 1000
hint: n up to 20 demands an in-place O(n^2) solution using matrix transpose and row-reversal pointers.
keywords: rotate the image by 90 degrees clockwise

hint: Small tree size (<= 100) allows a simple post-order or pre-order recursive child swap in O(n) time.
keywords: swapping the left and right subtrees
why_not: Right: Tree DFS recursively swaps left and right child pointers for every node in O(n) time and O(h) space. Not Tree BFS: Level-order traversal using a queue also swaps child pointers level by level in O(n) time, but requires extra queue space. Not Two Pointers: Linear pointer comparisons do not natively traverse hierarchical binary tree structures. Not 1D DP: Storing state subproblems is unnecessary for structural node child swapping.

title: Symmetric Tree
statement_short: Given the root of a binary tree, check whether it is a mirror of itself (i.e., symmetric around its center).
constraints: 0 <= number of nodes in tree <= 1000, -100 <= Node.val <= 100
hint: Small node count (<= 1000) permits a recursive top-down comparison of left and right subtrees in O(n) time.
why_not: Right: Tree DFS recursively compares opposite subtrees (left.left with right.right and left.right with right.left) in O(n) time and O(h) space. Not Tree BFS: Level-order traversal using a queue also checks symmetric node pairs in O(n) time, but requires extra queue space for tree width. Not Two Pointers: Scanning node pointers directly does not handle recursive tree branch comparisons naturally. Not 1D DP: Storing state subproblems is unnecessary for checking structural tree symmetry.

title: Construct Binary Tree from Preorder and Inorder Traversal
statement_short: Given two integer arrays preorder and inorder where preorder is the preorder traversal of a binary tree and inorder is the inorder traversal of the same tree, construct and return the binary tree.
constraints: 1 <= preorder.length <= 3000, inorder.length == preorder.length, -3000 <= preorder[i], inorder[i] <= 3000, preorder and inorder consist of unique values
hint: Unique values and length <= 3000 allow using a hash map for inorder index lookups to divide and conquer subtrees in O(n) time.
keywords: preorder traversal of a binary tree
inorder traversal of the same tree
why_not: Right: Tree DFS uses preorder elements as roots and splits inorder index segments via a hash map to recursively build left and right subtrees in O(n) time. Not Tree BFS: Level-order traversal queue logic cannot easily reconstruct tree topology from preorder root sequences. Not HashMap / Hash Set: HashMap accelerates index lookups, but the fundamental tree construction logic is recursive DFS division. Not Backtracking: Tree construction follows a deterministic split based on index lookups, requiring no exhaustive path searching.

title: Construct Binary Tree from Inorder and Postorder Traversal
statement_short: Given two integer arrays inorder and postorder where inorder is the inorder traversal of a binary tree and postorder is the postorder traversal of the same tree, construct and return the binary tree.
constraints: 1 <= inorder.length <= 3000, postorder.length == inorder.length, -3000 <= inorder[i], postorder[i] <= 3000, inorder and postorder consist of unique values
hint: Unique values and length <= 3000 allow using a hash map to locate root positions from the end of the postorder array in O(n) time.
keywords: inorder traversal of a binary tree
postorder traversal of the same tree
why_not: Right: Tree DFS picks roots backward from postorder array and partitions inorder segments using a hash map in O(n) time and O(n) space. Not Tree BFS: Level-order queue traversal does not align with postorder root selection sequence. Not HashMap / Hash Set: Hash maps store value-to-index mappings to optimize split lookups, but recursive DFS performs tree construction. Not 1D DP: Dynamic programming subproblem caching does not apply to recursive tree building.

title: Populating Next Right Pointers in Each Node II
statement_short: Given a binary tree, populate each next pointer to point to its next right node. If there is no next right node, the next pointer should be set to NULL.
constraints: 0 <= number of nodes in tree <= 6000, -100 <= Node.val <= 100
hint: Node count up to 6000 allows level-by-level traversal using next pointers of the previous level for O(1) space.
keywords: next pointer to point to its next right node
next pointer should be set to NULL
why_not: Right: Tree BFS traverses the tree level by level using a queue (or dummy head pointers for O(1) space) to connect adjacent right nodes in O(n) time. Not Tree DFS: DFS handles next pointers but requires careful order traversal and recursive stack memory. Not Linked List (Fast & Slow): Fast and slow pointers detect cycles rather than establishing cross-branch horizontal next pointers. Not Two Pointers: Scanning pointer pairs across non-linear structures fails without level-order tracking.

title: Flatten Binary Tree to Linked List
statement_short: Given the root of a binary tree, flatten the tree into a single right-skewed linked list in-place. The linked list should use the same TreeNode class where right pointer points to the next node and left pointer is always null, following preorder traversal order.
constraints: 0 <= number of nodes in tree <= 2000, -100 <= Node.val <= 100
hint: Small node count (<= 2000) permits reverse post-order recursion or Morris traversal for O(1) space flattening.
keywords: flatten the tree into a single right-skewed linked list in-place
why_not: Right: Tree DFS (reverse post-order: right, left, root) rewires left and right pointers into a preorder list in O(n) time and O(h) space (or Morris traversal for O(1) space). Not Tree BFS: Level-order traversal produces breadth-first ordering rather than the required preorder node sequence. Not Stack: Explicit stack iteration works, but recursive post-order DFS provides the standard topological rewiring logic. Not Two Pointers: Linear scanning pointers cannot navigate unflattened binary tree branches natively.

title: Path Sum
statement_short: Given the root of a binary tree and an integer targetSum, return true if the tree has a root-to-leaf path such that adding up all the values along the path equals targetSum. A leaf is a node with no children.
constraints: 0 <= number of nodes in tree <= 5000, -1000 <= Node.val <= 1000, -1000 <= targetSum <= 1000
hint: Node count up to 5000 allows recursive path sum subtraction from root to leaf in O(n) time.
keywords: adding up all the values along the path equals targetSum
why_not: Right: Tree DFS subtracts current node value from targetSum down to leaf nodes in O(n) time and O(h) space. Not Tree BFS: Level-order queue traversal tracking running node sums also works in O(n) time, but uses extra queue space. Not Prefix Sum: Prefix sums evaluate arbitrary subsegment sums, whereas path sum evaluates whole root-to-leaf paths. Not Backtracking: Backtracking collects all matching paths, whereas checking existence requires a simple boolean recursive check.

title: Sum Root to Leaf Numbers
statement_short: Given the root of a binary tree containing digits from 0 to 9 only, each root-to-leaf path represents a number. Return the total sum of all root-to-leaf numbers.
constraints: 1 <= number of nodes in tree <= 1000, 0 <= Node.val <= 9, depth of tree will not exceed 10
hint: Tree depth <= 10 and node count <= 1000 permit recursive digit accumulation (current \* 10 + val) in O(n) time.
keywords: total sum of all root-to-leaf numbers
why_not: Right: Tree DFS passes running path values (val \* 10 + node.val) down to leaf nodes and sums them in O(n) time and O(h) space. Not Tree BFS: Level-order queue traversal accumulates numbers per node in O(n) time, but requires extra queue space for node-value pairs. Not Math / Geometry: Digit shifting uses base-10 math, but the traversal backbone is tree recursion. Not Backtracking: Explicitly building and converting string digit lists adds unnecessary allocation overhead.

title: Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum
statement_short: Given the root of a binary tree, return the maximum path sum of any non-empty path. A path is defined as any sequence of nodes from parent to child or child to parent, where no node appears more than once.
constraints: 1 <= number of nodes in tree <= 3 \* 10^4, -1000 <= Node.val <= 1000
hint: Node count up to 3 \* 10^4 requires O(n) post-order DFS, updating global max with (left + right + root) while returning max single branch.
keywords: maximum path sum of any non-empty path
no node appears more than once
why_not: Right: Tree DFS computes maximum single-branch contribution from left and right subtrees post-order, updating global path sum in O(n) time and O(h) space. Not 1D DP: Dynamic programming state memoization on trees maps directly to post-order bottom-up DFS recursive returns. Not Tree BFS: Level-order traversal cannot calculate bottom-up subtree path gains easily. Not Prefix Sum: Prefix sums calculate path totals along straight ancestor lines, not paths turning at an arbitrary apex node.

title: Binary Search Tree Iterator
statement_short: Implement the BSTIterator class that represents an in-order iterator over a Binary Search Tree (BST). next() returns the next smallest number, and hasNext() returns whether a next number exists.
constraints: 1 <= number of nodes in tree <= 10^5, 0 <= Node.val <= 10^6, at most 10^5 calls to next and hasNext
hint: O(h) space requirement for iterator memory forbids storing all elements, demanding a controlled stack-based in-order traversal.
keywords: in-order iterator over a Binary Search Tree
why_not: Right: Stack maintains the current left-leaning path of unvisited BST nodes to achieve O(1) amortized next() time and O(h) auxiliary space. Not Tree DFS: Full recursive DFS traverses the entire tree at once rather than pausing and resuming on-demand across iterator calls. Not Two Pointers: Scanning pointer pairs requires linear indexing impossible on binary trees without array conversion. Not Heap / Priority Queue: Storing BST elements in a min-heap takes O(n) space and O(log n) next() time, ignoring BST order.

title: Count Complete Tree Nodes
statement_short: Given the root of a complete binary tree, return the number of the nodes in the tree. Design an algorithm that runs in less than O(n) time complexity.
constraints: 0 <= number of nodes in tree <= 5 \* 10^4, 0 <= Node.val <= 5 \* 10^4, tree is guaranteed to be complete
hint: Less than O(n) time mandate leverages complete tree properties to binary search existence of leaf nodes in O(log^2 n) time.
keywords: root of a complete binary tree
why_not: Right: Binary Search combined with tree height calculations tests leaf node existence in O(log^2 n) time, meeting the < O(n) constraint. Not Tree DFS: Standard recursive traversal visits every node in O(n) time, failing the required sub-linear time limit. Not Tree BFS: Level-order traversal queue visits all nodes in O(n) time and O(w) space. Not Math / Geometry: Formula 2^h - 1 calculates full tree node count, but leaf level gaps require binary search path checking.
complexity: O(log^2 n) time, O(log n) space

title: Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Tree
statement_short: Given a binary tree, find the lowest common ancestor of two given nodes p and q. The lowest common ancestor is defined as the lowest node in the tree that has both p and q as descendants.
constraints: 2 <= number of nodes in tree <= 10^5, -10^9 <= Node.val <= 10^9, p != q, p and q exist in the tree
hint: Node count up to 10^5 requires an O(n) post-order recursion, returning the current node when p or q is found.
keywords: has both p and q as descendants
why_not: Right: Tree DFS recursively checks left and right subtrees post-order, returning the root when p and q match opposite subtrees in O(n) time and O(h) space. Not Tree BFS: Level-order traversal using queue tracking requires storing parent pointers for all nodes using extra O(n) memory. Not Union-Find: Disjoint-set forest algorithms solve offline query batches, but post-order DFS directly finds LCA for single queries. Not Binary Search: The input is a general binary tree rather than a sorted binary search tree.

title: Binary Tree Right Side View
statement_short: Given the root of a binary tree, imagine yourself standing on the right side of it, return the values of the nodes you can see ordered from top to bottom.
constraints: 0 <= number of nodes in tree <= 100, -100 <= Node.val <= 100
hint: Small node count (<= 100) allows level-order traversal, capturing the last element of each queue level.
why_not: Right: Tree BFS traverses level by level, picking the last node in each level queue in O(n) time and O(w) space. Not Tree DFS: Pre-order (root-right-left) DFS works by tracking depth, but level-order BFS directly groups nodes by level. Not Two Pointers: Scanning pointer pairs cannot navigate hierarchical level structures natively. Not 1D DP: Subproblem state memoization does not apply to spatial tree view projections.

title: Average of Levels in Binary Tree
statement_short: Given the root of a binary tree, return the average value of the nodes on each level in the form of an array. Answers within 10^-5 of the actual answer will be accepted.
constraints: 1 <= number of nodes in tree <= 10^4, -2^31 <= Node.val <= 2^31 - 1
hint: Node count up to 10^4 permits level-by-level summation using a level-order queue traversal.
keywords: average value of the nodes on each level
why_not: Right: Tree BFS computes the sum of node values at each level and divides by level size in O(n) time and O(w) space. Not Tree DFS: DFS aggregates level sums using level-indexed lists, but BFS processes levels sequentially in memory. Not Prefix Sum: Prefix sums calculate range totals over arrays rather than level aggregates across binary trees. Not HashMap / Hash Set: Mapping levels to sums in a map works, but queue-based level processing is the natural BFS structure.

title: Binary Tree Level Order Traversal
statement_short: Given the root of a binary tree, return the level order traversal of its nodes' values (i.e., from left to right, level by level).
constraints: 0 <= number of nodes in tree <= 2000, -1000 <= Node.val <= 1000
hint: Small node count (<= 2000) permits queue-based breadth-first traversal grouping nodes by level depth.
keywords: left to right, level by level
why_not: Right: Tree BFS uses a queue to collect node values level by level from left to right in O(n) time and O(w) space. Not Tree DFS: Recursive DFS requires passing a level index to append values to sub-lists, whereas BFS visits levels sequentially. Not Stack: LIFO processing reverses node traversal order rather than preserving level order. Not 1D DP: Dynamic programming state caching does not apply to sequential tree level traversal.

title: Binary Tree Zigzag Level Order Traversal
statement_short: Given the root of a binary tree, return the zigzag level order traversal of its nodes' values (i.e., from left to right, then right to left for the next level and alternate between).
constraints: 0 <= number of nodes in tree <= 2000, -1000 <= Node.val <= 1000
hint: Small node count (<= 2000) allows level-order queue traversal with alternating direction inserts.
keywords: right to left for the next level and alternate
why_not: Right: Tree BFS uses a queue and reverses list output or uses a deque for odd-numbered levels in O(n) time and O(w) space. Not Tree DFS: DFS tracks depth and prepends elements for odd levels, but BFS maintains explicit level boundary queues. Not Two Pointers: Scanning pointer pairs cannot navigate non-linear level trees natively. Not Stack: Stack ordering handles single-direction depth traversal rather than alternating level directions.

title: Minimum Absolute Difference in BST
statement_short: Given the root of a Binary Search Tree (BST), return the minimum absolute difference between the values of any two different nodes in the tree.
constraints: 2 <= number of nodes in tree <= 10^4, 0 <= Node.val <= 10^5
hint: BST in-order traversal yields a sorted sequence, allowing single-pass adjacent value difference checks in O(n) time.
why_not: Right: Tree DFS performs in-order traversal to visit BST nodes in sorted order, keeping track of previous value in O(n) time and O(h) space. Not Binary Search: Binary searching for closest values per node takes O(n log n) time, which is slower than in-order DFS. Not Two Pointers: Array two pointers require copying all nodes into a sorted array first, using extra O(n) memory. Not Sorting: Extracting node values and sorting costs O(n log n) time, ignoring the pre-sorted BST property.

title: Kth Smallest Element in a BST
statement_short: Given the root of a binary search tree and an integer k, return the k-th smallest value (1-indexed) of all the values of the nodes in the tree.
constraints: 1 <= k <= n <= 10^4, 0 <= Node.val <= 10^4
hint: In-order traversal of a BST visits nodes in strictly increasing order, allowing stopping at the k-th node in O(k) time.
why_not: Right: Tree DFS performs in-order traversal to count visited nodes, returning immediately at the k-th element in O(h + k) time and O(h) space. Not Heap / Priority Queue: Storing node values in a max-heap takes O(n log k) time, ignoring the BST sorted property. Not Binary Search: Counting left subtree node size takes O(h^2) time unless node counts are stored in tree nodes. Not Two Pointers: Linear scanning pointers require indexed array access rather than BST node link traversal.

title: Validate Binary Search Tree
statement_short: Given the root of a binary tree, determine if it is a valid binary search tree (BST). A valid BST requires that all left descendants have strictly smaller values and all right descendants have strictly larger values.
constraints: 1 <= number of nodes in tree <= 10^4, -2^31 <= Node.val <= 2^31 - 1
hint: Node count up to 10^4 requires O(n) recursion, passing min and max valid bounds down to subtrees.
why_not: Right: Tree DFS recursively validates each node against min/max valid range boundaries (or checks strictly increasing order via in-order traversal) in O(n) time and O(h) space. Not Tree BFS: Level-order traversal checking range limits works in O(n) time, but requires extra queue memory for range tuples. Not Binary Search: Binary search locates elements, but validating full tree structure requires inspecting all nodes. Not Monotonic Stack: Monotonic stack checks array monotonicity rather than hierarchical subtree value bounds.

title: Number of Islands
statement_short: Given an m x n 2D binary grid grid which represents a map of '1's (land) and '0's (water), return the number of islands. An island is surrounded by water and is formed by connecting adjacent lands horizontally or vertically.
constraints: m == grid.length, n == grid[i].length, 1 <= m, n <= 300, grid[i][j] is '0' or '1'
hint: Grid size up to 300x300 permits O(m \* n) traversal, sinking visited land cells using BFS/DFS.
keywords: connecting adjacent lands horizontally or vertically
why_not: Right: Graph BFS traverses connected land cells level by level using a queue, mutating visited cells to '0' in O(m \* n) time and O(min(m, n)) space. Not Graph DFS: DFS using recursion also sinks islands in O(m \* n) time, but risks stack overflow on deep grid components without iterative stack. Not Union-Find: Disjoint sets track connected land components in O(m \* n \* alpha(m\*n)) time, which adds auxiliary parent array memory. Not 2D DP: Dynamic programming requires directional subproblem ordering, failing for arbitrary 4-directional connected components.
complexity: O(m \* n) time, O(min(m, n)) space

title: Surrounded Regions
statement_short: Given an m x n matrix board containing 'X' and 'O', capture all regions that are 4-directionally surrounded by 'X'. A region is captured by flipping all 'O's into 'X's in that surrounded region.
constraints: m == board.length, n == board[i].length, 1 <= m, n <= 200, board[i][j] is 'X' or 'O'
hint: Grid up to 200x200 permits O(m \* n) time by starting traversals from boundary 'O' cells to mark non-surrounded regions.
why_not: Right: Graph BFS starts from boundary 'O' cells, traversing connected un-capturable land cells into temporary markers before flipping remaining 'O's to 'X's in O(m \* n) time. Not Graph DFS: Recursive DFS works but can cause call-stack overflow on large grids. Not Union-Find: Disjoint sets link border nodes to dummy components in O(m \* n \* alpha(n)) time, but uses extra parent memory. Not 2D DP: Grid DP requires directional state flow, failing for 4-directional boundary component reachability.
complexity: O(m \* n) time, O(m \* n) space

title: Clone Graph
statement_short: Given a reference of a node in a connected undirected graph, return a deep copy of the graph. Each node contains a value and a list of its neighbors.
constraints: 0 <= number of nodes <= 100, 1 <= Node.val <= 100, no repeated edges or self-loops
hint: Small node count (<= 100) allows level-by-level queue traversal while mapping original nodes to cloned nodes.
why_not: Right: Graph BFS traverses connected graph nodes using a queue and map to create node clones in O(V + E) time and O(V) space. Not HashMap / Hash Set: Using a hash map stores original-to-clone node mappings, but requires graph traversal (BFS/DFS) to explore all edges. Not Union-Find: Disjoint sets partition connected components rather than deep copying graph nodes and edges. Not Tree DFS: Tree recursion assumes hierarchical acyclic parent-child links, whereas arbitrary graphs require handling cycles.

title: Evaluate Division
statement_short: Given equations of variable divisions and an array of values, answer query divisions between variables. Return -1.0 if a division query cannot be determined.
constraints: 1 <= equations.length <= 20, 1 <= queries.length <= 20, values.length == equations.length, 0.0 < values[i] <= 20.0
hint: Small query limits allow constructing a weighted directed graph and evaluating path products per query.
why_not: Right: Graph DFS traverses variable edge paths to accumulate multiplicative weight ratios in O(Q \* (V + E)) time. Not Union-Find: Disjoint sets with weight tracking also solve query ratios in O((V + E) + Q \* alpha(V)) time, but graph traversal directly models path multiplication. Not 1D DP: Dynamic programming state caching does not handle arbitrary graph query paths without precomputing Floyd-Warshall all-pairs matrices. Not Two Pointers: Scanning pointer pairs cannot navigate non-linear weighted ratio edges.
complexity: O(Q \* (V + E)) time, O(V + E) space

title: Course Schedule
statement_short: There are numCourses courses you must take, labeled from 0 to numCourses - 1\. Given prerequisite pairs [a, b] where course b must be taken before course a, determine if it is possible to finish all courses.
constraints: 1 <= numCourses <= 2000, 0 <= prerequisites.length <= 5000, prerequisites[i].length == 2, all pairs are unique
hint: Prerequisite constraints up to 2000 courses mandate detecting cycles in a directed dependency graph.
keywords: course b must be taken before course a
why_not: Right: Topological Sort (Kahn's in-degree BFS or DFS cycle detection) checks for directed cycles in dependency order in O(V + E) time. Not Graph BFS: Standard unweighted BFS explores reachable levels, but topological sort specifically tracks in-degree dependencies and cycle detection. Not Union-Find: Disjoint sets detect undirected graph cycles, but fail to track directed edge dependencies effectively. Not 1D DP: Linear DP memoization does not resolve cyclic dependency graph structures.
complexity: O(V + E) time, O(V + E) space

title: Course Schedule II
statement_short: Given the total number of courses numCourses and a list of prerequisite pairs, return the ordering of courses you should take to finish all courses. Return an empty array if it is impossible to finish all courses.
constraints: 1 <= numCourses <= 2000, 0 <= prerequisites.length <= 5000, prerequisites[i].length == 2, all pairs are unique
hint: Dependencies up to 2000 nodes require constructing a valid linear order of directed graph nodes.
keywords: empty array if it is impossible
why_not: Right: Topological Sort uses Kahn's algorithm (in-degree queue) to output a valid linear ordering of graph nodes in O(V + E) time. Not Graph DFS: Standard DFS traverses graph paths but requires post-order stack reversal to produce topological node ordering. Not Tree BFS: Level-order tree traversal assumes hierarchical parent-child nodes rather than arbitrary directed graph edges. Not Backtracking: Permutating all node sequences causes TLE compared to linear topological sorting.
complexity: O(V + E) time, O(V + E) space

title: Snakes and Ladders
statement_short: Given an n x n board where squares are labeled 1 to n^2 in a Boustrophedon style, find the minimum number of moves to reach square n^2\. Some squares contain snakes or ladders that destination-jump players upon landing.
constraints: 2 <= n <= 20, board[i][j] is -1 or between 1 and n^2
hint: Small board dimension (n <= 20) allows unweighted shortest path search from square 1 to n^2 using queue traversal.
why_not: Right: Graph BFS finds the shortest path on an unweighted game board grid in O(n^2) time and O(n^2) space. Not 1D DP: Board moves contain snakes that create backward edges (cycles), causing infinite loops in standard DP. Not Backtracking: Exploring all dice roll sequences causes exponential TLE. Not Heap / Priority Queue: Priority queues add O(log N) overhead when edge weights are all uniformly equal to 1.

title: Minimum Genetic Mutation
statement_short: Given a start gene string, an end gene string, and a gene bank array, return the minimum number of mutations needed to mutate startGene to endGene. Each mutation changes a single character and must be a valid gene in bank.
constraints: startGene.length == endGene.length == 8, 0 <= bank.length <= 10, bank[i].length == 8, genes consist of 'A', 'C', 'G', 'T'
hint: Small bank length (<= 10) and fixed string length 8 allow finding the shortest path in a state graph via queue traversal.
why_not: Right: Graph BFS finds the shortest transformation path in an unweighted gene state graph in O(N \* L) time. Not Backtracking: Backtracking explores all valid gene paths recursively but does not guarantee finding the shortest path first without full state tree exhaustion. Not Trie: Trie stores string dictionaries, but does not calculate shortest mutation distances between words. Not Two Pointers: Gene strings are unordered, preventing two-pointer linear matching.

title: Word Ladder
statement_short: Given two words beginWord and endWord, and a dictionary wordList, return the number of words in the shortest transformation sequence from beginWord to endWord such that each adjacent word differs by single letter.
constraints: 1 <= beginWord.length <= 10, endWord.length == beginWord.length, 1 <= wordList.length <= 5000, wordList[i].length == beginWord.length
hint: Dictionary size up to 5000 permits finding the shortest path in an unweighted word graph using level-order queue search.
why_not: Right: Graph BFS finds the shortest path level by level in an unweighted word transition graph in O(N \* M^2) time. Not Graph DFS: DFS explores deep paths first, requiring searching the entire state space to guarantee shortest path length. Not Trie: Prefix trees speed up single-character word dictionary lookups but do not manage shortest path level traversal queues. Not 1D DP: Word transformations form general graph edges rather than linear DAG state transitions.
complexity: O(N \* M^2) time, O(N \* M) space

title: Implement Trie (Prefix Tree)
statement_short: Implement a Trie with insert(word), search(word), and startsWith(prefix) methods. search returns true if word is in the trie, and startsWith returns true if there is a previously inserted word with the given prefix.
constraints: 1 <= word.length, prefix.length <= 2000, word and prefix consist of lowercase English letters, at most 3 \* 10^4 calls
hint: Efficient string prefix matching and retrieval mandates a tree data structure where nodes represent individual characters.
keywords: previously inserted word with the given prefix
why_not: Right: Trie stores characters at child nodes, enabling O(L) time insertion, word search, and prefix matching. Not HashMap / Hash Set: Hash sets support O(L) exact word lookup, but cannot perform O(L) prefix matching without checking all stored keys. Not Binary Search: Binary search on a sorted string array checks prefixes in O(L log N) time, which is slower than linear Trie traversal. Not Tree DFS: General binary trees do not organize character edges for multi-child prefix branches.
complexity: O(L) time per operation, O(N \* L) space

title: Design Add and Search Words Data Structure
statement_short: Design a data structure that supports adding new words and searching if a string matches any previously added string. Search queries may contain '.' dots, where '.' can match any single letter.
constraints: 1 <= word.length <= 25, word in addWord consists of lowercase English letters, word in search consists of '.' or lowercase letters, at most 10^4 calls
hint: Word length up to 25 with wildcard '.' matching favors a character trie combined with recursive DFS branch exploration.
why_not: Right: Trie combined with recursive child branching for '.' dot characters evaluates wildcard prefix queries in O(L) best-case time. Not HashMap / Hash Set: Storing words in a hash set handles exact lookups in O(L), but wildcard '.' searches require checking every stored word in O(N \* L) time. Not Backtracking: Exhaustive string pattern matching without a prefix tree requires scanning the full dictionary. Not Two Pointers: Scanning pointers cannot match character wildcards across multi-branch dictionaries natively.
complexity: O(L) time for add, O(26^L) worst for wildcard search, O(N \* L) space

title: Word Search II
statement_short: Given an m x n board of characters and a list of strings words, return all words on the board. Each word must be constructed from sequentially adjacent cells horizontally or vertically, without reusing any cell.
constraints: m == board.length, n == board[i].length, 1 <= m, n <= 12, 1 <= words.length <= 3 \* 10^4, 1 <= words[i].length <= 10
hint: Grid up to 12x12 and 3 \* 10^4 target words mandate storing words in a Trie to prune DFS backtracking paths early.
why_not: Right: Trie coupled with 2D grid DFS backtracking prunes invalid prefix paths instantly in O(M \* N \* 4^L) worst-case time. Not Backtracking: Pure backtracking without a Trie searches for each of the 30,000 words independently on the grid, causing severe TLE. Not Graph BFS: Level-order grid traversal requires storing full path histories per queue item, taking excessive memory. Not HashMap / Hash Set: Hash sets check complete words, but cannot prune grid search paths at non-matching prefixes.
complexity: O(M \* N \* 4^L) time, O(W \* L) space

title: Letter Combinations of a Phone Number
statement_short: Given a string containing digits from 2-9 inclusive, return all possible letter combinations that the number could represent. Return the answer in any order, mapping each digit to its corresponding telephone keypad letters.
constraints: 0 <= digits.length <= 4, digits[i] is a digit from '2' to '9'
hint: Tiny input size (digits.length <= 4) implies search space is small, favoring recursive combination generation.
why_not: Right: Backtracking recursively generates all decision tree paths mapping digits to letter choices in O(4^n) time. Not Tree DFS: DFS traverses fixed existing tree structures rather than building combinations dynamically. Not 1D DP: Dynamic programming caches subproblems, whereas generating all combinations requires full path exploration. Not HashMap / Hash Set: Hash tables map digits to letters, but combination generation requires recursive backtracking.

hint: Subproblem overlap (ways(n) = ways(n-1) + ways(n-2)) dictates state memoization or space-optimized dynamic programming.

Not Backtracking: Exhaustive recursive search computes subproblems redundantly, causing TLE in O(2^n) time. Not Math / Geometry: Binet Fibonacci formula computes answer in O(log n), but 1D DP is the core subproblem memoization pattern. Not Greedy: Local step choices do not calculate global path count totals.

title: House Robber
statement_short: Given an integer array nums representing the amount of money at each house, return the maximum amount of money you can collect without selecting two adjacent elements.
constraints: 1 <= nums.length <= 100, 0 <= nums[i] <= 400
hint: Optimal subproblem state choice at index i is max(dp[i-1], dp[i-2] + nums[i]), demanding linear dynamic programming.
keywords: amount of money at each house
why_not: Right: 1D DP maintains max sum choices (selecting current element vs skipping current element) in O(n) time and O(1) space. Not Greedy: Picking the highest value element locally fails to maximize sum across non-adjacent combinations. Not Backtracking: Trying all select/skip combinations takes exponential O(2^n) time. Not Two Pointers: Scanning pointers cannot balance non-adjacent subproblem state transitions.

title: Word Break
statement_short: Given a string s and a dictionary of strings wordDict, return true if s can be segmented into a space-separated sequence of one or more dictionary words. The same word in the dictionary may be reused multiple times.
constraints: 1 <= s.length <= 300, 1 <= wordDict.length <= 1000, 1 <= wordDict[i].length <= 20, s and wordDict[i] consist of lowercase English letters, all strings of wordDict are unique
hint: String length up to 300 permits checking if prefix s[0..i] is breakable using subproblem boolean state dp[j].
why_not: Right: 1D DP records whether prefix s[0..i] can be segmented into valid words using dp[j] && wordDict.contains(s[j..i]) in O(n^2 \* k) time. Not Trie: Trie speeds up dictionary word match checks, but verifying full string segmentation relies on dynamic programming state transitions. Not Backtracking: Recursive partitioning without memoization leads to TLE with O(2^n) exponential time. Not Sliding Window: Word lengths in the sequence vary, preventing fixed/monotonic sliding window movement.

title: Coin Change
statement_short: Given an integer array coins representing coins of different denominations and an integer amount representing a total amount of money, return the fewest number of coins that you need to make up that amount. Return -1 if that amount cannot be made up.
constraints: 1 <= coins.length <= 12, 1 <= coins[i] <= 2^31 - 1, 0 <= amount <= 10^4
hint: Target amount up to 10^4 requires computing minimum coins for each sub-amount up to amount using dynamic programming.
why_not: Right: 1D DP computes minimum coins needed for each amount i from 1 to target (dp[i] = min(dp[i], dp[i-coin] + 1)) in O(amount \* n) time. Not Greedy: Greedy picking largest coins fails for non-canonical coin systems (e.g. coins [1, 3, 4] for amount 6). Not Graph BFS: Shortest path BFS on an amount state graph works, but 1D DP array updates are the standard unbounded knapsack pattern. Not Backtracking: Exploring all coin combinations recursively causes TLE.

title: Longest Increasing Subsequence
statement_short: Given an integer array nums, return the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence. Follow up: Can you come up with an algorithm that runs in O(n log n) time complexity?
constraints: 1 <= nums.length <= 2500, -10^4 <= nums[i] <= 10^4
hint: Array size up to 2500 can be solved in O(n^2) via 1D DP or O(n log n) by maintaining tail values with binary search.
keywords: runs in O(n log n) time complexity
why_not: Right: 1D DP (or DP with Binary Search Patience Sorting) tracks longest increasing subsequence endings in O(n log n) time and O(n) space. Not Binary Search: Binary search is used within Patience Sorting to find substitution positions, but the underlying problem is finding LIS subproblem state. Not Two Pointers: Subsequences are non-contiguous, so linear two-pointer scanning cannot evaluate non-adjacent elements. Not Monotonic Stack: Monotonic stack tracks next greater elements, but cannot handle arbitrary element replacements in LIS.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space

title: Triangle
statement_short: Given a triangle array, return the minimum path sum from top to bottom. For each step, you may move to adjacent numbers on the row below.
constraints: 1 <= triangle.length <= 200, triangle[i].length == i + 1, -10^4 <= triangle[i][j] <= 10^4
hint: Triangle length up to 200 permits bottom-up grid state transitions to compute min path sum.
keywords: adjacent numbers on the row below
why_not: Right: 2D DP computes minimum path sums bottom-up by taking min(dp[row+1][col], dp[row+1][col+1]) + triangle[row][col] in O(n^2) time and O(n) space. Not Graph BFS: Level-order grid queue search works, but 2D DP handles overlapping subproblem states directly. Not Greedy: Picking the smaller adjacent element locally fails when a larger node leads to smaller overall path sums later. Not Backtracking: Exploring all paths recursively takes exponential O(2^n) time.

title: Minimum Path Sum
statement_short: Given a m x n grid filled with non-negative numbers, find a path from top left to bottom right which minimizes the sum of all numbers along its path. You can only move either down or right at any point in time.
constraints: m == grid.length, n == grid[i].length, 1 <= m, n <= 200, 0 <= grid[i][j] <= 200
hint: Grid bounds up to 200x200 permit 2D grid state memoization computing min incoming path totals.
keywords: minimizes the sum of all numbers along its path
only move either down or right
why_not: Right: 2D DP tracks min path sum at each grid cell using min(dp[r-1][c], dp[r][c-1]) + grid[r][c] in O(m \* n) time and O(n) space. Not Graph BFS: Dijkstra shortest path queue algorithm works, but 2D grid DP avoids priority queue overhead. Not Greedy: Moving to the smaller neighbor cell locally misses optimal paths with smaller future cells. Not Backtracking: Exploring all grid paths recursively takes exponential O(2^(m+n)) time.

title: Unique Paths II
statement_short: Given an m x n integer array obstacleGrid, return the number of possible unique paths from the top-left corner to the bottom-right corner. Movement is restricted to down or right, and obstacles marked as 1 cannot be traversed.
constraints: m == obstacleGrid.length, n == obstacleGrid[i].length, 1 <= m, n <= 100, obstacleGrid[i][j] is 0 or 1
hint: Grid bounds up to 100x100 permit 2D DP path accumulation, setting blocked obstacle cells to 0 ways.
keywords: obstacles marked as 1 cannot be traversed
why_not: Right: 2D DP accumulates path counts from top and left neighbors, setting obstacle cells to 0 in O(m \* n) time and O(n) space. Not Graph BFS: Queue-based grid traversal counts path ways, but 2D DP handles state tabulation without queue management memory. Not Backtracking: Recursive path exploration without state memoization causes TLE in O(2^(m+n)) time. Not Math / Geometry: Combinatorial formula C(m+n-2, m-1) calculates obstacle-free paths, but fails when arbitrary obstacle grids block paths.

title: Longest Palindromic Substring
statement_short: Given a string s, return the longest palindromic substring in s.
constraints: 1 <= s.length <= 1000, s consists of only digits and English letters
hint: String length up to 1000 permits checking center expansion for odd and even palindrome lengths.
why_not: Right: Two Pointers expands outward from each character center (odd and even lengths) in O(n^2) time and O(1) space. Not 2D DP: 2D DP stores boolean palindrome states dp[i][j] in O(n^2) time but consumes O(n^2) auxiliary memory. Not Sliding Window: Palindromes expand symmetrically from centers rather than maintaining a monotonic window. Not HashMap / Hash Set: Hash sets check substring existence but do not verify symmetrical palindrome ordering.

title: Interleaving String
statement_short: Given strings s1, s2, and s3, find whether s3 is formed by an interleaving of s1 and s2\. An interleaving of two strings preserves the relative order of characters from each string.
constraints: 0 <= s1.length, s2.length <= 100, 0 <= s3.length <= 200, s1, s2, and s3 consist of lowercase English letters
hint: Lengths up to 100 allow 2D DP grid state dp[i][j] tracking prefix character matches of s1 and s2 against s3.
keywords: formed by an interleaving of s1 and s2
preserves the relative order of characters
why_not: Right: 2D DP memoizes whether s1[0..i] and s2[0..j] interleave into s3[0..i+j] in O(m \* n) time and O(n) space. Not Two Pointers: Greedy pointer matching fails when both s1 and s2 contain matching characters, requiring backtracking state choices. Not Backtracking: Exploring string matching choices recursively without memoization causes TLE with exponential time complexity. Not HashMap / Hash Set: Character frequency counts verify anagrams but lose relative sequence ordering.

title: Edit Distance
statement_short: Given two strings word1 and word2, return the minimum number of operations required to convert word1 to word2\. You can insert, delete, or replace a character.
constraints: 0 <= word1.length, word2.length <= 500, word1 and word2 consist of lowercase English letters
hint: Word lengths up to 500 allow 2D DP matrix matching min operations across character prefixes.
keywords: insert, delete, or replace a character
why_not: Right: 2D DP computes Levinshtein distance matrix matching insert, delete, and replace subproblems in O(m \* n) time and O(n) space. Not Two Pointers: Scanning pointer pairs cannot handle multi-operation insertions and deletions without state grid transitions. Not Greedy: Local character matching choices fail because early edits impact global edit distance costs. Not Backtracking: Recursive branch exploration without memoization causes TLE with 3^(m+n) exponential complexity.

title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock IV
statement_short: Given an integer array prices where prices[i] is the price of a given stock on the i-th day, and an integer k, return the maximum profit you can achieve by completing at most k transactions.
constraints: 1 <= k <= 100, 1 <= prices.length <= 1000, 0 <= prices[i] <= 1000
hint: Transaction count k up to 100 and prices length 1000 favor 2D state matrix (transactions and holding state).
why_not: Right: 2D DP tracks max profit for t transactions holding or not holding stock on day i in O(n \* k) time and O(k) space. Not Greedy: Local price delta accumulation works for unrestricted transactions (k >= n/2), but bounded k requires state DP. Not Two Pointers: Scanning pointer pairs from ends cannot evaluate multi-transaction capacity constraints. Not Backtracking: Exploring buy/sell decision combinations recursively leads to TLE with exponential time complexity.

title: Maximal Square
statement_short: Given an m x n binary matrix filled with 0's and 1's, find the largest square containing only 1's and return its area.
constraints: m == matrix.length, n == matrix[i].length, 1 <= m, n <= 300, matrix[i][j] is '0' or '1'
hint: Grid dimensions up to 300x300 favor 2D DP computing min(top, left, top-left) + 1 square side lengths.
why_not: Right: 2D DP calculates max square side ending at (r, c) using min(dp[r-1][c], dp[r][c-1], dp[r-1][c-1]) + 1 in O(m \* n) time and O(n) space. Not Monotonic Stack: Monotonic stack finds largest rectangle in histogram in O(m \* n) time, but square bounds are solved more cleanly with 2D DP. Not Graph BFS: Connected component traversal checks island shapes, but does not calculate max square side length. Not Two Pointers: Scanning pointer pairs from grid borders cannot verify internal square 1s fill efficiently.
